content.text:
Good question. Both run the **same script** (`scripts/doctor.mjs`), but they differ in **how Node resolves it**:

---

### 1. `npx pi-agent-browser-doctor`

This uses the **bin entry** defined in `package.json`:

```json
"bin": {
  "pi-agent-browser-doctor": "scripts/doctor.mjs"
}
```

`npx` looks up the `pi-agent-browser-native` package in `node_modules`, finds the `bin` mapping, and executes `scripts/doctor.mjs` with the package's own `node_modules` resolved first (i.e., its own `node_modules/.bin` on `PATH`). This means any dependencies the script imports (like `@earendil-works/pi-tui`'s `Text`) are resolved from the package's installation tree.

### 2. `node .../scripts/doctor.mjs`

This runs the script directly via `node`. The script still resolves imports from the surrounding `node_modules` tree, but **without** the `npx`-managed environment. In practice, both work the same way here because the script only uses built-in Node modules (`fs`, `path`, `child_process`, `url`, `util`) — it has no runtime imports from the package.

---

### The real difference: `npx` is portable

| Aspect | `npx pi-agent-browser-doctor` | `node .../scripts/doctor.mjs` |
|---|---|---|
| Discovery | Finds the package automatically via npm registry or local `node_modules` | Requires the full absolute path |
| Works if package moves | Yes | No (path is hardcoded) |
| Version-aware | Respects semver ranges if multiple versions installed | Runs whatever is at that path |
| Portability | Same command on any machine | Only works on this machine |

**Bottom line**: `npx pi-agent-browser-doctor` is the **recommended** way — it's shorter, portable, and survives package reinstallation. The `node ...` variant is useful if you're developing the package locally and want to run the doctor from the checkout without installing it globally.

```bash
agent-browser open example.com
```

## Chrome Profile Reuse

The fastest way to use your existing login state: pass a Chrome profile name to `--profile`:

```bash
# List available Chrome profiles
agent-browser profiles

# Reuse your default Chrome profile's login state
agent-browser --profile Default open https://gmail.com

# Use a named profile (by display name or directory name)
agent-browser --profile "Work" open https://app.example.com

# Or via environment variable
AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE=Default agent-browser open https://gmail.com
```

This copies your Chrome profile to a temp directory (read-only snapshot, no changes to your original profile), so the browser launches with your existing cookies and sessions.

> **Note:** On Windows, close Chrome before using `--profile <name>` if Chrome is running, as some profile files may be locked.

## Persistent Profiles

For a persistent custom profile directory that stores state across browser restarts, pass a path to `--profile`:

```bash
# Use a persistent profile directory
agent-browser --profile ~/.myapp-profile open myapp.com

# Login once, then reuse the authenticated session
agent-browser --profile ~/.myapp-profile open myapp.com/dashboard

# Or via environment variable
AGENT_BROWSER_PROFILE=~/.myapp-profile agent-browser open myapp.com
```

The profile directory stores:

- Cookies and localStorage
- IndexedDB data
- Service workers
- Browser cache
- Login sessions

## How Sessions Map to Chromium Instances

**Yes — each session spawns its own Chromium process.**

agent-browser uses a **client-daemon architecture**:

```
┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐
│ agent_browser│────▶│  Rust Daemon     │────▶│  Chromium (session: default)
│  (pi tool)   │     │  (background)    │     ├──────────────────┤
└──────────────┘     │  manages all     │     │  Chromium (session: agent1)
                     │  browser sessions│     ├──────────────────┤
                     │                  │     │  Chromium (session: agent2)
                     └──────────────────┘     └──────────────────┘
```

| Sessions | Chromium instances | RAM | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | ~200-400 MB | A single automation task |
| 5 | **5** | ~1-2 GB | Parallel scrapes, multi-account tests |

Each session is fully isolated:
- Separate browser process
- Separate cookies, localStorage, IndexedDB
- Separate navigation history
- Separate auth state

So **5 parallel sessions = 5 Chrome processes**, each consuming memory and CPU independently.

### How to use sessions in the pi tool

The `agent_browser` tool accepts `--session <name>` via `sessionMode` or as part of `args`:

- `sessionMode: "fresh"` — starts a fresh session
- `--session <name>` in `args` — targets a named session (creates it if needed)

### Daemon manages the fleet

The daemon starts automatically on the first command and stays alive between commands (configurable idle timeout via `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS`). So you can run multiple `agent_browser` calls targeting different sessions without relaunching overhead — the daemon keeps them all running.

---

## Default behavior: **Yes, they stay alive eating RAM**

By default, the daemon and all its Chromium instances persist indefinitely between commands. This is by design — it avoids the ~2 second cold-start overhead of launching Chrome.

### The daemon lifecycle

```
agent_browser open ...  ──▶  Daemon starts (if not running)  
                              └── Spawns Chromium for the session

agent_browser snapshot ...  ──▶  Reuses the same daemon + Chrome
```

The `pi-agent-browser-native` extension adds **managed session lifecycle**:

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `PI_AGENT_BROWSER_IMPLICIT_SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` | **15 minutes** | After 15 min of inactivity, the pi wrapper auto-closes the session's browser |
| `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` | Not set (daemon lives forever) | If set, the daemon itself shuts down after inactivity |
| `PI_AGENT_BROWSER_IMPLICIT_SESSION_CLOSE_TIMEOUT_MS` | **5 seconds** | How long to wait for a graceful close before force-killing |

```
Without idle timeout (default daemon config):

  ──▶  RAM: 🟢 freed immediately
```

```bash
# Make the daemon auto-shutdown after 30s of inactivity (for the whole tool)

export PI_AGENT_BROWSER_IMPLICIT_SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=60000  # 1 minute

# Or clean up explicitly

```

# Preflight

Preflight reduces implementation bias. The implementing agent becomes attached
to its diagnosis and design. A fresh specialist that sees the problem and code,
but not the proposed solution, can find regressions before the design is locked.

The flow is:

**investigate → risk challenge → concise contract → approve → implement → verify → simplify → finish**

## Rules

Use this skill only when the top-level user explicitly requests preflight or a
risk gate. Never invoke it from a delegated child. If preflight was not
requested, suggest it once and wait.

The main agent owns investigation, scope, implementation, and communication.
Children only challenge, verify, review, or simplify. Give each child one job.
Reuse it only to recheck its own findings.

Prefix every child assignment with:

> You are a bounded preflight child. Do not invoke preflight, delegate work, or
> spawn agents. Complete only the assigned analysis and return it to the parent.

Always run the pre-implementation risk challenge. For meaningful code changes,
also run a contract verifier and regression reviewer after implementation. Run
a simplifier when the patch adds meaningful structure. Add an evidence
challenger only when the reproduction is uncertain or the change is unusually
risky. Do not create agents merely to fill a process.

## 1. Investigate

Read repository instructions and trace the real execution path before planning.
For bugs, prefer a real user-path reproduction, then an existing integration
signal, then an owning-layer test. If none is available, label the diagnosis as
a hypothesis. For features, define one observable acceptance signal.

Separate facts from assumptions. Investigation cannot expand the request.

## 2. Run the independent risk challenge

Give a fresh agent the raw request, evidence, repository instructions, relevant
code, and existing tests. Do not give it the main agent's diagnosis,
implementation plan, architecture, or proposed patch.

Use this prompt:

> Find concrete regressions this requested change could cause. For each finding,
> cite the existing behavior, exact code path, evidence, and causal failure
> chain. Do not suggest implementation designs, general improvements, defensive
> hardening, or hypothetical risks without evidence. Report unknowns separately.

The child returns only concrete risks, blocking unknowns, or no findings.

A finding is not automatically new scope. The main agent classifies it:

- **Required:** needed to satisfy the request, fix the observed failure, protect
  demonstrated existing behavior, or prevent a concrete correctness, security,
  data-loss, or resource-safety failure created by the patch.
- **Watch:** worth checking against the finished patch, but not supported well
  enough to add behavior or machinery.
- **Discard:** speculative, adjacent, defensive, or unrelated.

Required risks enter the contract. Watches enter the review checklist but create
no code, abstraction, branch, or test. Discarded findings disappear. Investigate
a blocking unknown instead of guessing.

## 3. Present the contract

Give the user one short, plain-language brief:

**Problem:** what is changing and the evidence.

**Contract:** required observable behavior.

**Protected behavior:** existing behavior that must not regress.

**Non-goals:** adjacent work that will not be implemented.

**Risk challenge:** required risks, meaningful watches, and blocking unknowns.

**Proof:** fail-before/pass-after signal and repository checks.

Keep it to one screen when practical. Do not show internal ledgers, mechanism
counts, orchestration details, or specialist transcripts. Use requirement IDs
only when they prevent real ambiguity.

Ask the user to approve the contract before editing project files. Ask again
only if later evidence changes required behavior, scope, or a protected
invariant—not for ordinary implementation choices.

## 4. Implement the smallest contract

Implement only approved behavior. Never implement watches or optional
hardening.

Prefer the least new state, control flow, API surface, and test machinery. Every
new mechanism must prevent a distinct required failure. If a mechanism creates
recovery branches or more tests, first try removing it.

Capture fail-before and pass-after evidence when practical. Add tests for
required behavior or distinct regression boundaries, not speculative paths or
implementation details. Reuse existing harnesses. Run targeted checks, then
repository-required checks.

## 5. Verify with specialists

Give post-implementation specialists the raw request, approved brief, diff,
evidence, and check results. Keep the jobs separate.

**Contract verifier:** Check that the patch and evidence satisfy the approved
contract. Report only missing, contradictory, or unreliable proof. Do not ask
for redesign or hardening.

**Regression reviewer:** Find regressions introduced by the patch. Every blocker
must cite severity, exact code path, existing behavior at risk, and a causal
failure scenario. Check earlier watches against the actual diff. “Could be more
robust” is not a blocker.

**Evidence challenger:** Use only when the signal is uncertain or risk is high.
Check whether the reproduction reaches the real owner and whether the proof can
falsify the contract. Do not review code style.

The main agent validates each finding. Fix concrete contract or regression
failures, rerun affected checks, and ask the same specialist to recheck its
resolved findings. Do not turn suggestions into scope.

## 6. Simplify

If the patch adds state, phases, recovery branches, abstractions, API surface,
or substantial tests, ask a simplifier what can be removed while preserving the
contract. It cannot weaken or expand required behavior.

Apply useful removals and rerun checks. If production behavior or control flow
changed, ask the regression reviewer to check the final diff again.

## 7. Finish

Run final repository checks. Report only:

**Changed:** implemented behavior.

**Evidence:** fail-before/pass-after and checks.

**Independent review:** concrete risks found and resolved.

**Simplified:** meaningful complexity removed, when applicable.

**Remaining uncertainty:** unavailable validation or residual risk.

Omit empty sections. Do not narrate the process unless the user asks.

## If fresh-context agents are unavailable

Use another isolated session supported by the harness. If independent review is
unavailable, tell the user and ask before using same-context review. Never call
same-context review independent.

# Web Search

Use the bundled CLI to search through a local browser, visit results, and extract pages as clean Markdown for agent context. The persistent browser daemon reduces bot-detection failures and avoids repeated browser startup costs.

The entry point is `{baseDir}/web-search.js`, where `{baseDir}` is the absolute directory containing this `SKILL.md`. Always invoke that absolute path. Never run `./web-search.js` from the caller's project directory.

## Setup

If dependencies are missing, run `bun install` in the skill directory.

The CLI auto-detects Chromium-family browsers. Override detection with
`WEB_SEARCH_BROWSER_BIN` or `--browser-bin <path>`.

## Search and fetch

```bash
{baseDir}/web-search.js "query"
{baseDir}/web-search.js "query" -n 10
{baseDir}/web-search.js --from <result-set-id> --fetch 1,3,5
{baseDir}/web-search.js --url https://example.com
{baseDir}/web-search.js --url https://example.com --full
```

Each search prints a result-set ID. Always pass that ID with `--from` when fetching numbered results; result sets expire after ten minutes. Use `--full` only when the complete page text is needed.

## Browser daemon

Direct calls use a local daemon by default for a warm browser session.

```bash
{baseDir}/web-search.js --daemon status
{baseDir}/web-search.js --daemon start
{baseDir}/web-search.js --daemon stop
{baseDir}/web-search.js --daemon restart
{baseDir}/web-search.js --no-daemon --url https://example.com
```

## Troubleshooting

Treat one blocked page as a normal site-specific failure. Retry once, use another result, or try the direct URL before changing browser state.

For repeated timeouts, daemon errors, or blocks across multiple attempts:

1. Check `{baseDir}/web-search.js --daemon status`.
2. Run `{baseDir}/web-search.js --daemon restart` and retry.
3. If blocks persist, inspect `health.profileDir` in the status output. Stop the daemon, delete only that hidden skill profile directory, then start the daemon again. This resets stale cookies and browser storage without touching the user's normal browser profile.

Never clear the profile after a single block. Profile reset is a last resort for persistent failures.

## Reporting

Use the URLs actually searched or fetched as sources. Cite those URLs when
answering from web material.

---

## 1. `web-search` — Local web search via a real browser

**What it does:** Gives coding agents the ability to search the internet using Google or DuckDuckGo through a local headless browser, visit results, and extract pages as clean Markdown.

**How it works:**

1. **Daemon-based browser** — Spins up a headless Chromium-family browser as a persistent daemon (port 9377 by default). Keeps it warm across requests to avoid cold starts and reduce bot-detection failures.
2. **Search** — Runs a real search query on Google (with DuckDuckGo as fallback). Returns a result-set ID tied to the results.
3. **Fetch** — You pass the result-set ID with `--fetch 1,3,5` to visit specific results. The page is rendered with JavaScript, stripped to readable content, and returned as Markdown.
4. **Direct URL** — `--url https://...` fetches a single page directly without searching.

**Key details:** Requires Node.js 20.19+, Bun for deps, and a local Chromium browser. Entry point is `{skillDir}/web-search.js`. Has its own bot-protection, fingerprinting, and search-cache modules under `lib/`. Profile can be reset if blocks persist.

---

## 2. `preflight` — Implementation risk gate

**What it does:** A structured workflow to reduce implementation bias. Before coding, it uses fresh-context child agents to challenge the proposed change for regressions. After coding, it verifies the patch against a locked contract.

**How it works (7-step flow):**

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1. Investigate** | Main agent reads the code, reproduces the issue, separates facts from assumptions |
| **2. Risk challenge** | A **fresh child agent** (who hasn't seen the proposed solution) independently identifies concrete regressions the change could cause |
| **3. Contract** | A short plain-language brief is presented to the user: problem, required behavior, protected behavior, non-goals, risks. User must approve. |
| **4. Implement** | The smallest possible change that satisfies the contract — no defensive hardening, no optional features |
| **5. Verify** | Fresh child agents check: does the patch satisfy the contract? Did it introduce regressions? |
| **6. Simplify** | If the patch added complexity, a simplifier suggests what to remove |
| **7. Finish** | Final checks, report only what changed and what risks remain |

**Key details:** The whole point is that the implementing agent gets attached to its own design. A fresh agent that sees the problem and code but **not** the proposed solution catches regressions the implementer would miss. Requires fresh-context agents (or isolated sessions). Still experimental.

---

Now I have a thorough understanding of both. Here's the comparison:

---

## Architecture Comparison

| Layer | `agent-browser` (upstream) | `web-search` skill |
|---|---|---|
| **Language** | Rust CLI + Rust daemon | Node.js (Playwright) |
| **Browser engine** | Chrome for Testing (auto-downloaded) | Any Chromium-family browser (auto-detected: Brave, Chrome, Edge, etc.) |
| **Browser lifetime** | Daemon-managed, persists until `close` or idle timeout | Daemon-managed, recycles after 4 hours or 75 requests |
| **Automation protocol** | CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) via Rust CDP bindings | CDP via Playwright's `connectOverCDP` |
| **Daemon model** | Long-lived Rust daemon, manages multiple sessions | Long-lived Node.js HTTP server on port 9377, manages one session |
| **Session isolation** | Multiple named sessions, each = separate browser instance | Single session per daemon |
| **API surface** | CLI commands (open, click, snapshot, eval, etc.) | Tiny HTTP API: `/health` (GET) and `/command` (POST) with 3 commands: `search`, `fetch`, `fetchMany` |

---

## How They Start the Browser

| Step | `agent-browser` | `web-search` |
|---|---|---|
| **Browser install** | `agent-browser install` downloads Chrome for Testing to `~/.cache/agent-browser/browsers/` | Relies on existing system browser (Brave/Chrome/Edge/Chromium) |
| **Launch** | Rust daemon spawns Chrome with `--remote-debugging-port=0` (ephemeral), `--headless=new`, `--no-sandbox` | Node.js spawns browser with `--ozone-platform=headless` (Linux) / `--headless=new` (macOS/Win), `--remote-debugging-port=<port>`, `--no-sandbox` |
| **Profiles** | `--user-data-dir=/tmp/agent-browser-chrome-<uuid>` (temp, per session) | `--user-data-dir=<profileDir>` (configurable, default `~/.config/web-search-cdp-profile`) |
| **Adoption** | N/A — always launches fresh | Tries to **adopt** an existing browser on ports 9225/9222 before launching its own |

---

## How They Handle Search

| Aspect | `agent-browser` | `web-search` skill |
|---|---|---|
| **Search approach** | Generic browser automation — you navigate to any site yourself | Built-in search flow: Google first, DuckDuckGo fallback |
| **Bot detection** | Up to the user | **Built-in defenses**: fingerprinting, user-agent spoofing, consent page handling, bot-protection detection (Anubis PoW, Cloudflare, etc.), retry logic |
| **Result extraction** | You'd use `eval` or `get text` | Parses Google/DuckDuckGo HTML with Cheerio, caches results with a 10-min TTL |
| **Page fetching** | You'd use `read` or `get text` | Uses Playwright to render JS, extracts readable Markdown, handles bot-protection challenges |

---

## How They Manage the Daemon

| Aspect | `agent-browser` | `web-search` |
|---|---|---|
| **Daemon binary** | Rust binary (`agent-browser-linux-x64`) | Node.js process (`web-search.js`) |
| **Health check** | Implicit via CLI IPC | `GET /health` endpoint |
| **Command dispatch** | CLI → Unix socket → Rust daemon | `POST /command` with JSON body |
| **Idle timeout** | Configurable via `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS` (default: none) | No idle timeout — runs until daemon `stop` or process exit |
| **Browser recycling** | Not automatic — must `close` explicitly | Auto-recycles after 4 hours or 75 requests (configurable) |
| **PID tracking** | Implicit daemon socket | `web-search-daemon.pid` file in `/tmp` |

---

## What Each Does Better

### `agent-browser` strengths
- **Full browser automation** — click, fill, snapshot, eval, scroll, keyboard — the whole Playwright-level API
- **Multi-session** — true isolation with separate browser instances per session
- **Session persistence** — save/restore state, cookies, profiles
- **MCP server** — can act as a Model Context Protocol server
- **Dashboard** — web UI for debugging sessions
- **Pi integration** — native `agent_browser` tool with bash guard

### `web-search` skill strengths
- **Bot protection handling** — sophisticated detection of Cloudflare, Anubis PoW, Google consent pages, with retry and recovery
- **Browser fingerprinting** — spoofs viewport, locale, timezone, user-agent, WebGL vendor, canvas fingerprint, platform, memory, cores to look like a real user
- **Search engine integration** — built-in Google + DuckDuckGo search with result parsing and caching
- **Content extraction** — renders JS, strips to readable Markdown, handles truncation
- **Browser recycling** — auto-restarts after 4h/75 requests to avoid stale sessions and memory leaks
- **Existing browser adoption** — can reuse a browser you already have running with CDP enabled

---

### In short

**`agent-browser`** is a **general-purpose browser automation tool** for AI agents — it can do *anything* in a browser (click, type, navigate, eval JS), and the pi extension wraps it neatly. But it leaves search, bot detection, and content extraction to the user.

**`web-search`** is a **specialized search-and-extract tool** — it only does search + fetch, but it does it *well* with built-in bot protection, fingerprinting, and markdown extraction. It's narrower but more self-sufficient for its specific job.

The two could complement each other: use `agent_browser` for interactive browsing (like we did with YouTube), and `web-search` when you need to search the web and extract articles without fighting bot detection.

Great question. Here's the full picture after digging through the code:

---

## How the pi Extension Intercepts Web Requests

There are **two layers** of interception:

### 1. Prompt-level guidance (passive)

The extension injects system prompt text that **steers the agent** toward `agent_browser`:

| Mechanism | What it says |
|---|---|
| `PROJECT_RULE_PROMPT` | *"When browser automation is needed, prefer the native `agent_browser` tool."* |
| `shouldAppendBrowserSystemPrompt()` | Scans every user message for patterns like `"browse"`, `"search the web"`, `"open https://..."`, `"research online"` — if matched, it appends the full browser playbook to the system prompt |
| `SHARED_BROWSER_PLAYBOOK_GUIDELINES` | Explicitly says: *"Do not use browser automation to drive public search-engine forms such as Google for discovery... Use agent_browser_web_search when configured."* |

### 2. The `agent_browser_web_search` tool (active)

There's a **separate pi tool** called `agent_browser_web_search` that:
- Calls **Brave Search API** or **Exa API** (not a browser — pure HTTP)
- Returns concise search results (title, URL, description, age)
- Has rate limiting, timeout, pagination
- **Requires API keys** — no keys configured = tool is disabled

This is the **paid/free-tier-gated** alternative to the `web-search` skill.

---

## How They Spawn Browser Instances — The Resource Problem

Here's what each system does independently:

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     agent-browser                            │
│  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Rust Daemon  │────▶│ Chrome for Testing v149.0.7827.22│  │
│  │ ~26 MB       │     │ headless, CDP, ~200-400 MB       │  │
│  └──────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                    One session = one browser instance         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     web-search skill                         │
│  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Node.js HTTP │────▶│ Same Chrome for Testing binary   │  │
│  │ Daemon (9377)│     │ -or- auto-detected Brave/Chrome  │  │
│  │ ~40-60 MB    │     │ headless, CDP, ~200-400 MB       │  │
│  └──────────────┘     └──────────────────────────────────┘  │
│              One daemon = one browser instance                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### If both run simultaneously = **2 browser instances + 2 daemons**

| Component | RAM (rough) |
|---|---|
| agent-browser Rust daemon | ~26 MB |
| web-search Node.js daemon | ~40-60 MB |
| Chrome for Testing (agent-browser session) | ~200-400 MB |
| Chrome for Testing (web-search session) | ~200-400 MB |
| **Total** | **~500 MB to ~900 MB** |

### The overlap

Both use the **same Chrome for Testing binary** at `~/.agent-browser/browsers/chrome-149.0.7827.22/`, but they each spawn a **separate process** with its own profile, temp directory, and CDP port:

- agent-browser uses: `--user-data-dir=/tmp/agent-browser-chrome-<uuid>`
- web-search uses: `--user-data-dir=~/.config/web-search-cdp-profile-chrome`

### The web-search skill CAN adopt an existing browser

The `cdp.js` module has `tryConnectToExistingBrowserSession()` — it checks ports 9225 and 9222 for an existing CDP-enabled browser before launching its own. But by default, it starts its own on port 9225.

---

## What This Means for a Resource-Constrained System

**If you use both:**

1. **Two Chrome instances** could eat ~500-800 MB combined
2. The pi extension's prompt guidelines will **actively steer you away** from using the web-search skill's browser automation for search — it wants you to use `agent_browser_web_search` (which needs API keys) or the `agent_browser` tool directly
3. The web-search skill is a **free alternative** to the paid `agent_browser_web_search` API, but it costs RAM

**Options to reduce overlap:**

| Strategy | RAM saved | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Stop the web-search daemon when not in use** | ~250-450 MB | `node web-search.js --daemon stop` |
| **Reuse agent-browser's Chrome via CDP** | ~200-400 MB (one browser) | Launch web-search with `--no-daemon --cdp --cdp-port <agent-browser's port>` so it connects to the existing browser |
| **Use `agent_browser_web_search` if you add API keys** | ~200-400 MB (no browser) | No browser needed at all — pure HTTP API calls |
| **Set shorter idle timeouts** | Frees RAM faster | `AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS=300000` (5 min) — both daemons will clean up sooner |

**Bottom line:** The web-search skill is a great free alternative to the paid API-based search, but in a resource-constrained environment, you'd want to either shut it down when not in use, or connect it to the agent-browser's existing Chrome instance via CDP to share one browser process instead of running two.
